content: Sodium perborate (PBS) is a white, odorless, water-soluble chemical compound with the chemical formula NaBO3. It can crystallize in two forms: as a monohydrate or as a tetrahydrate. The production of sodium perborate involves a chemical reaction between sodium tetraborate, hydrogen peroxide, and sodium hydroxide. It is known to be a skin irritant. Unlike percarbonate and perphosphate, sodium perborate is not merely a compound formed by the addition of peroxide. Instead, it contains true peroxygen bonds, which contribute to its enhanced stability and make it safer to handle and store. The monohydrate form of sodium perborate dissolves more readily in water compared to the tetrahydrate form and exhibits greater thermal stability. The monohydrate is typically prepared by heating the tetrahydrate. When sodium perborate comes into contact with water, it undergoes hydrolysis, releasing hydrogen peroxide and borate. This property makes it a source of active oxygen, which is utilized in various applications, including detergents, laundry detergents, cleaning products, and laundry bleaches. It is also an ingredient in some tooth-bleaching formulations. Sodium perborate possesses antiseptic properties and can function as a disinfectant. Additionally, it is used as a disappearing preservative in certain brands of eye drops. For example, Novartis, a manufacturer of eye drops, claims that sodium perborate turns into pure water and oxygen upon contact with your eye. Sodium perborate is considered a less aggressive bleaching agent compared to sodium hypochlorite, as it causes less degradation to dyes and textiles. Borates, which are part of its composition, also exhibit some non-oxidative bleaching properties. At temperatures exceeding 60°C, sodium perborate releases oxygen rapidly. To activate it at lower temperatures (40–60°C), it must be combined with an appropriate activator, such as tetraacetylethylenediamine (TAED).
